text: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is Microsoft's commercial EDR platform, and it's built on the same ideas from the last lesson: continuous telemetry, behavioral detection, and the ability to respond. This lesson stays at the concept level — onboarding, alerts, incidents, and automated investigation — rather than walking through a specific portal screen, since those change release to release.

Before a device shows up anywhere in Defender for Endpoint, it has to be onboarded — registered with the Defender tenant so its sensor starts reporting. Modern Windows versions ship with that sensor built in; it just needs to be configured and pointed at a tenant, which admins typically do through Group Policy, Microsoft Intune, or Microsoft Configuration Manager at scale, rather than one device at a time.

Locally, Defender Antivirus is one signal feeding that same sensor, and you can check it with real PowerShell cmdlets: Get-MpComputerStatus reports whether real-time protection is on and signatures are current, Get-MpThreatDetection lists what's been found on that machine, and Get-MpPreference shows the configured scan and exclusion settings. Defender for Endpoint layers behavioral EDR telemetry on top of that same antivirus engine, rather than replacing it.

Each onboarded device streams activity to the cloud service, which raises an alert whenever something looks suspicious. A real intrusion rarely produces just one alert, though — it produces many, often across several devices, as an attacker moves laterally. Defender for Endpoint automatically correlates related alerts into a single incident, so an analyst sees one attack story instead of dozens of disconnected, unrelated-looking tickets.

Automated investigation and remediation takes that correlation a step further. For many alert types, the system automatically investigates — checking the file, the process tree, and related artifacts — reaches a verdict of malicious, suspicious, or benign, and for high-confidence malicious verdicts can remediate on its own, quarantining a file or killing a process without waiting for a human to act first. Lower-confidence verdicts get queued for analyst review instead.

That combination — onboarding at scale, alert-to-incident correlation, and automated remediation — is what lets a small SOC team cover a large fleet of endpoints without drowning in individual alerts. Next, we'll look at the other side of a mixed environment: what endpoint protection looks like on Linux.
